entry.title: Building Bulletproof Social Media Import Pipelines: Designing UX That Survives API Failures
entry.summary:
Last quarter, our platform dropped 40,000 imported Instagram posts because a third-party rate limit threw a silent 429 error and our frontend loader spun happily into infinity. If your social media import pipeline relies on synchronous HTTP requests, naive spinners, and blind optimism, you are one network glitch away from alienating your power users and corrupting your database state. When we build content import features, we tend to treat them like simple file uploads. We throw a drag-and-drop zone on the screen, hook up an endpoint, and assume the external social network's API will happily stream gigabytes of media without breaking a sweat. In reality, external APIs are fragile, rate-limited, heavily paginated, and prone to sudden schema shifts.

entry.title: The Retry Storm Problem: Why Your ASP.NET Core API Needs Idempotency Keys
entry.summary:
The Retry Storm Problem: How Idempotency Keys Save Your ASP.NET Core API
Introduction
Every .NET developer knows the frustration of a failed request followed by an automatic retry. But there's a subtler danger: when those retries hit side-effecting endpoints (payment processing, email dispatch, inventory updates), you can end up with duplicate charges, duplicate notifications, or corrupted state. This is the "retry storm" problem—and it's solved with idempotency keys. Consider a mobile client that experiences a brief network glitch while placing an order. The HTTP request times out, the client library retries, and because our API doesn't track whether an operation has already been executed, both attempts succeed. entry.title: Travel weeks break publishing more often than talent does
entry.summary: Sales trips and on-site weeks don’t usually kill writing skill. They kill cadence. The public page stays stuck on last quarter’s announcement while the person who “owns the blog” lives in airports. Market shortcuts—pay-per-post on a rented account—feel efficient until nobody is home to approve facts. Then the trail goes quiet again, and search looks like the company took leave. A more durable setup is a thin, agreed capacity: facts list from the traveler, draft and images from a helper, publish only to accounts the company authorizes. Some public pages describe that bundle; price and scope are whatever the site currently states—no promised leads. Measure the boring thing: three weeks away, can a stranger still find a recent, accurate intro? If not, the gap isn’t inspiration. It’s process. Guanji Notes. People can travel; the trail should still update on purpose.
